claim: The hippocampal region plays a pivotal role in spatial and episodic memory.
source: The hippocampal region plays a pivotal role in spatial and episodic memory (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Morris et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978 and Morris et al., 1982

claim: Different stages of memory processing are associated with distinct brain states and are characterized by distinct oscillatory patterns of the hippocampal local field potential.
source: The different stages of memory processing (Marr, 1971; Buzsáki, 1989) are associated with distinct brain states and are characterized by distinct oscillatory patterns of the hippocampal local field potential (LFP) (Buzsáki et al., 1983; Colgin, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marr, 1971; Buzsáki, 1989; Buzsáki et al., 1983; and Colgin, 2016

claim: Place cells of the hippocampus are activated in a sequence that corresponds to the order in which the animal visits their preferred spatial locations during exploration.
source: When rodents explore their environment, place cells of the hippocampus are activated in a sequence that corresponds to the order in which the animal visits their preferred spatial locations (place fields) (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971

claim: The same sequences of firing activity can be identified on a faster time scale during individual cycles of the 4–10 Hz theta oscillation.
source: The same sequences of firing activity can also be identified, on a faster time scale, during individual cycles of the 4–10 Hz theta oscillation that dominates the hippocampal LFP in this state (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Foster and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; and Foster and Wilson, 2007

claim: Compressed sequences during theta oscillation are thought to be optimal for learning via activity-dependent synaptic plasticity.
source: These compressed sequences are thought to be optimal for learning via activity-dependent synaptic plasticity (Jensen and Lisman, 2005; Foster and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jensen and Lisman, 2005 and Foster and Wilson, 2007

claim: Slow-wave sleep and quiet wakefulness are characterized by the repetitive but irregular occurrence of bursts of activity in the hippocampus, marked by sharp waves and associated high-frequency ripple oscillations.
source: Other behavioral states such as slow-wave sleep and quiet wakefulness are characterized by the repetitive but irregular occurrence of bursts of activity in the hippocampus, marked by the appearance of sharp waves (Buzsáki et al., 1983; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994) and associated high-frequency (150–220 Hz) ripple oscillations (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Buzsáki et al., 1992) in the LFP.
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzsáki et al., 1983; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; and Buzsáki et al., 1992

claim: Disruption of SWRs impairs long-term memory.
source: Disruption of SWRs was shown to impair long-term memory (Girardeau et al., 2009; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010; Jadhav et al., 2012; Oliva et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Girardeau et al., 2009; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010; Jadhav et al., 2012; and Oliva et al., 2020

claim: Activity sequences observed during exploration are recapitulated during SWRs in the absence of any apparent external driver.
source: The activity sequences observed during exploration are also recapitulated during SWRs (Nádasdy et al., 1999; Kudrimoti et al., 1999; Lee and Wilson, 2002), in the absence of any apparent external driver, and this 'replay' can happen either in the same or in a reversed order relative to the original behaviorally driven sequence (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Csicsvari et al., 2007; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Gupta et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nádasdy et al., 1999; Kudrimoti et al., 1999; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Csicsvari et al., 2007; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; and Gupta et al., 2010

claim: Awake replay is predominantly in the forward direction near choice points during navigation.
source: More specifically, awake replay is predominantly in the 'forward' direction near choice points during navigation (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013), while it is mainly 'backward' when the animal encounters a reward (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Diba and Buzsáki, 2007 and Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013

claim: Awake replay is mainly backward when the animal encounters a reward.
source: More specifically, awake replay is predominantly in the 'forward' direction near choice points during navigation (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013), while it is mainly 'backward' when the animal encounters a reward (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Diba and Buzsáki, 2007

claim: Sleep replay is suggested to be involved in memory consolidation.
source: Consequently, while sleep replay was suggested to be involved in memory consolidation, forward and reverse replay in awake animals may contribute to memory recall and reward-based learning, respectively (Carr et al., 2011; Foster, 2017; Pfeiffer, 2017; Olafsdottir et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carr et al., 2011; Foster, 2017; Pfeiffer, 2017; and Olafsdottir et al., 2018

claim: Forward and reverse replay in awake animals may contribute to memory recall and reward-based learning, respectively.
source: Consequently, while sleep replay was suggested to be involved in memory consolidation, forward and reverse replay in awake animals may contribute to memory recall and reward-based learning, respectively (Carr et al., 2011; Foster, 2017; Pfeiffer, 2017; Olafsdottir et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carr et al., 2011; Foster, 2017; Pfeiffer, 2017; and Olafsdottir et al., 2018

claim: Behavioral tasks with a high memory demand led to an increase in the duration of SWRs.
source: Finally, behavioral tasks with a high memory demand led to an increase in the duration of SWRs, while artificial prolongation of SWRs improved memory (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019

claim: Artificial prolongation of SWRs improved memory.
source: Finally, behavioral tasks with a high memory demand led to an increase in the duration of SWRs, while artificial prolongation of SWRs improved memory (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019

claim: Area CA3 of the hippocampus has been proposed to be a critical site for hippocampal memory operations due to the presence of an extensive set of modifiable excitatory recurrent connections.
source: For several decades, area CA3 of the hippocampus has been proposed to be a critical site for hippocampal memory operations, mainly due to the presence of an extensive set of modifiable excitatory recurrent connections that could support the storage and retrieval of activity patterns and thus implement long-term memory (Marr, 1971; McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Levy, 1996; Rolls, 1996; Káli and Dayan, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marr, 1971; McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Levy, 1996; Rolls, 1996; and Káli and Dayan, 2000

claim: Area CA3 is strongly involved in the generation of SWRs and the associated forward and reverse replay.
source: Area CA3 was also shown to be strongly involved in the generation of SWRs and the associated forward and reverse replay (Buzsáki, 2015; Davoudi and Foster, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2015 and Davoudi and Foster, 2019

claim: The model network contained 8000 PCs and 150 PVBCs, corresponding roughly to the size of the CA3 area in a 600-µm-thick slice of the mouse hippocampus.
source: The complete network consisted of 8000 excitatory pyramidal cells (PCs) and 150 inhibitory parvalbumin-containing basket cells (PVBCs), corresponding roughly to the size of the CA3 area in a 600-µm-thick slice of the mouse hippocampus, which is known to be capable of generating SWRs (Hájos et al., 2013; Schlingloff et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hájos et al., 2013 and Schlingloff et al., 2014

claim: PCs and PVBCs are indispensable to the generation of SWRs.
source: These two cell types are known to be indispensable to the generation of SWRs (Rácz et al., 2009; Ellender et al., 2010; English et al., 2014; Schlingloff et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2014; Gulyás and Freund, 2015; Buzsáki, 2015; Gan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rácz et al., 2009; Ellender et al., 2010; English et al., 2014; Schlingloff et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2014; Gulyás and Freund, 2015; Buzsáki, 2015; and Gan et al., 2017

claim: All neurons in the network were modeled as single-compartment, adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire models whose parameters were fit to reproduce in vitro voltage traces.
source: All neurons in the network were modeled as single-compartment, adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire (AdExpIF) models whose parameters were fit to reproduce in vitro voltage traces of the given cell types in response to a series of step current injections ('Materials and methods' and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Describes the modeling approach and fitting to experimental data

claim: During the exploration phase, the spiking activity of PCs was explicitly set to mimic the firing patterns of a population of place cells during simulated runs on a linear track.
source: During the exploration phase, the spiking activity of PCs was explicitly set to mimic the firing patterns of a population of place cells during simulated runs on a linear track, and the recurrent connections between PCs evolved according to an experimentally constrained, spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) rule (see below).
evidence: Describes the simulation methodology

claim: The recurrent connections between PCs evolved according to an experimentally constrained, spike-timing-dependent plasticity rule.
source: During the exploration phase, the spiking activity of PCs was explicitly set to mimic the firing patterns of a population of place cells during simulated runs on a linear track, and the recurrent connections between PCs evolved according to an experimentally constrained, spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) rule (see below).
evidence: Describes the learning mechanism in the model

claim: The most prominent feature of the learned recurrent excitatory synaptic weight matrix was its highly organized structure with relatively few strong synapses near the diagonal.
source: The most prominent feature of the learned recurrent excitatory synaptic weight matrix was its highly organized structure (Figure 1C). Relatively few strong (>1 nS) synapses near the diagonal (representing pairs of cells with overlapping place fields) emerged from a background of much weaker connections.
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 1C

claim: Spontaneously generated activity in the network consisted of alternating periods of low activity and high activity, which resembled the recurring appearance of sharp wave events during slow-wave sleep and quiet wakefulness.
source: Spontaneously generated activity in the network consisted of alternating periods of low activity (mean PC rates below 1 Hz) and high activity (mean PC rates around 3.5 Hz), which resembled the recurring appearance of sharp wave events during slow-wave sleep and quiet wakefulness (Figure 2A).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2A

claim: High-activity events in the model were accompanied by transient oscillations in the ripple frequency range.
source: Similar to experimental sharp waves, high-activity events in the model were accompanied by transient oscillations in the ripple frequency range (Figure 2B; Buzsáki, 1986; Buzsáki et al., 1992; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2B, compared to experimental findings cited

claim: Ripple oscillations were reliably present in the estimated LFP during the high-activity periods.
source: We calculated an estimate of the LFP by summing the synaptic inputs of a small, randomly selected subset of PCs (Mazzoni et al., 2008), and found that ripple oscillations were reliably present in this signal during the high-activity periods (Figures 1D and 2B).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figures 1D and 2B

claim: Place cell sequences were replayed during simulated SWRs.
source: When we plotted the spike times of all PCs with place cells ordered according to the location of their place fields on the track during the learning phase, it became clear that place cell sequences were replayed during simulated SWRs, while activity had no obvious structure in the low-activity periods between SWRs (Figure 2A).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2A

claim: Replay of place cell sequences could occur in either the forward or the backward direction relative to the order of activation in the learning phase.
source: Interestingly, replay of place cell sequences could occur in either the forward or the backward direction relative to the order of activation in the learning phase (Figure 2A).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2A

claim: Simultaneous forward and backward replay was never observed in the model.
source: Importantly, apart from some initial transients, simultaneous forward and backward replay was never observed.
evidence: Observation from the model simulations

claim: The network model reproduced the broad, long-tailed step-size distribution in the sequence of decoded locations during SWRs, as observed experimentally.
source: Interestingly, our network model also reproduced the broad, long-tailed step-size distribution in the sequence of decoded locations during SWRs, as observed experimentally by Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015; Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, compared to experimental findings from Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015

claim: Both PCs and PVBCs received approximately balanced excitation and inhibition during SWR events.
source: At the level of single cells, we found that both PCs and PVBCs received approximately balanced excitation and inhibition during SWR events, and inhibitory currents were modulated at the ripple frequency in these periods (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D

claim: Inhibitory currents were modulated at the ripple frequency during SWR events.
source: At the level of single cells, we found that both PCs and PVBCs received approximately balanced excitation and inhibition during SWR events, and inhibitory currents were modulated at the ripple frequency in these periods (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D

claim: Excitatory inputs dominated between SWRs and during the initiation of SWR events.
source: Excitatory inputs dominated between SWRs and during the initiation of SWR events.
evidence: Observation from the model simulations

claim: Only a small minority of PCs fired in individual ripple cycles.
source: Only a small minority of PCs fired in individual ripple cycles, while the participation of PVBCs was much higher (but not complete), resulting in a mean PVBC firing rate of ∼65 Hz during the SWRs, which is much higher than their baseline rate, but significantly below the ripple frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B

claim: The participation of PVBCs in ripple cycles was much higher than PCs but not complete, resulting in a mean PVBC firing rate of ∼65 Hz during the SWRs.
source: Only a small minority of PCs fired in individual ripple cycles, while the participation of PVBCs was much higher (but not complete), resulting in a mean PVBC firing rate of ∼65 Hz during the SWRs, which is much higher than their baseline rate, but significantly below the ripple frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B

claim: The findings regarding balanced excitation/inhibition and ripple-frequency modulation were consistent with experimental results in vitro and in vivo.
source: All of these findings were consistent with experimental results in vitro (Hájos et al., 2013; Schlingloff et al., 2014) and in vivo (Varga et al., 2012; English et al., 2014; Hulse et al., 2016; Gan et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison to experimental findings cited

claim: Ripple oscillations had higher power and appeared at lower multiplier levels in the PVBC population than in the PC population.
source: Ripple oscillations had higher power and appeared at lower multiplier levels in the PVBC population than in the PC population (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that they originate from the PVBCs and propagate to the PCs, in agreement with theories based on experimental findings (Buzsáki et al., 1992; Ylinen et al., 1995; Rácz et al., 2009; Schlingloff et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2014; Gan et al., 2017).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, compared to experimental findings cited

claim: Ripple oscillations originate from the PVBCs and propagate to the PCs.
source: Ripple oscillations had higher power and appeared at lower multiplier levels in the PVBC population than in the PC population (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that they originate from the PVBCs and propagate to the PCs, in agreement with theories based on experimental findings (Buzsáki et al., 1992; Ylinen et al., 1995; Rácz et al., 2009; Schlingloff et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2014; Gan et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference from model observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, supported by citations

claim: It is possible to store the representations of multiple environments in the weight matrix.
source: Next, we showed that it is possible to store the representations of multiple environments in the weight matrix, and this change does not fundamentally alter the network dynamics (Figure 4).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 4

claim: During each SWR event after learning two environments, a place cell sequence from either one or the other environment was reactivated.
source: The resulting population-level dynamics was quite similar to the one following experience in a single environment, but, during each SWR event, a place cell sequence from either one or the other environment was reactivated (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: The experimentally determined symmetric STDP rule is necessary for bidirectional replay.
source: First, in order to gauge the significance of the experimentally determined symmetric STDP rule, we changed the STDP kernel to the classical asymmetric one that characterizes many other connections in the nervous system (Figure 5A–C; Bi and Poo, 1998; Gerstner et al., 2014). In this case, the learned weight matrix was reminiscent of the feedforward chains that characterized several of the earlier models of hippocampal replay (Jahnke et al., 2015; Chenkov et al., 2017; Theodoni et al., 2018). We found that this weight structure also supported the generation of SWR events and the reactivation of learned sequences in our model; however, crucially, sequence replays occurred only in the forward direction (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Observation from the model manipulation shown in Figure 5, compared to baseline model

claim: The asymmetric STDP rule resulted in sequence replays occurring only in the forward direction.
source: We found that this weight structure also supported the generation of SWR events and the reactivation of learned sequences in our model; however, crucially, sequence replays occurred only in the forward direction (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Observation from the model manipulation shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: The fine structure of recurrent excitation not only enables coding (sequence replay), but also has a major effect on the global average network dynamics in hippocampal area CA3.
source: Taken together, these modifications suggest that, unlike in the model of Omura et al., 2015, the distribution of the excitatory recurrent synaptic weights is neither necessary nor sufficient for the observed physiological population activity in our model. In other words, our simulation results suggest that the fine structure of recurrent excitation not only enables coding (sequence replay), but also has a major effect on the global average network dynamics (firing rates, sharp waves, and ripple oscillations) in hippocampal area CA3.
evidence: Inference from model manipulations (binarized and shuffled weight matrices)

claim: Cellular adaptation is necessary for replay in the model.
source: To test this hypothesis, we refitted our single-cell data on PC responses to current injections using a modified ExpIF model that did not contain any adaptation mechanism (but was otherwise similar to the baseline model). Although the nonadapting ExpIF model provided a reasonably good fit to our single-cell data (Figure 7A), and the weights resulting from learning were identical to the baseline case, the spontaneous network dynamics was completely different: there was no sequence replay for any scaling of the recurrent PC-PC weights; instead, when structured activity emerged from the random background, it was in the form of a stationary rather than a moving bump (Figure 7B). Therefore, it was the combination of a symmetric learning rule with cellular adaptation that created the possibility of bidirectional replay in our network model.
evidence: Observation from the model manipulation shown in Figure 7

claim: The combination of a symmetric learning rule with cellular adaptation created the possibility of bidirectional replay in the network model.
source: Therefore, it was the combination of a symmetric learning rule with cellular adaptation that created the possibility of bidirectional replay in our network model.
evidence: Inference from model manipulations comparing symmetric STDP with and without adaptation

claim: Ripple oscillations can be disentangled from sequence replays and only require sufficient drive to the interconnected PVBC population.
source: From the weight matrix modifications, we also learned that ripple oscillations can be disentangled from sequence replays and only require sufficient drive to the interconnected PVBC population in our model (Figure 6F).
evidence: Observation from the model manipulation shown in Figure 6F

claim: Ripple oscillations emerged when the net excitatory drive to PVBCs was sufficiently large.
source: We found that ripple oscillations emerged when the net excitatory drive to PVBCs (which is proportional to the product of the incoming weight and the presynaptic firing rate) was sufficiently large.
evidence: Observation from the simplified PVBC network simulation

claim: Above the threshold for ripple generation, the properties of the oscillation depended only mildly on the strength of the input.
source: Above this threshold, the properties of the oscillation depended only mildly on the strength of the input (e.g., the frequency of the oscillation increased moderately with increasing drive), and the firing of PVBCs was synchronized mainly by the decay of inhibitory synaptic current evoked by shared input from their peers.
evidence: Observation from the simplified PVBC network simulation

claim: Recurrent inhibitory connections were both necessary and sufficient for the generation of ripple oscillations in the model.
source: Taken together, these results support the conclusions of previous modeling (Brunel and Wang, 2003; Geisler et al., 2005; Taxidis et al., 2012; Donoso et al., 2018; Ramirez-Villegas et al., 2018) as well as experimental studies (Buzsáki et al., 1992; Ylinen et al., 1995; Rácz et al., 2009; Ellender et al., 2010; Schlingloff et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2014; Gulyás and Freund, 2015; Gan et al., 2017), proposing that ripple oscillations are generated in strongly driven, recurrently connected inhibitory networks by the fast inhibitory neuronal oscillation (FINO) mechanism. In fact, recurrent inhibitory connections were both necessary and sufficient for the generation of ripple oscillations in our model.
evidence: Observation from model manipulations, supported by citations to previous modeling and experimental studies

claim: Structured (learned) recurrent excitation in the CA3 region not only enables coding and memory, but is critical for the generation of SWRs as well.
source: Our principal findings from analyzing and manipulating this model are as follows: (1) structured (learned) recurrent excitation in the CA3 region not only enables coding and memory, but is critical for the generation of SWRs as well
evidence: Summary of findings from model manipulations

claim: The symmetric STDP rule, in combination with cellular adaptation in CA3 PCs, provides an explanation for the coexistence of forward and reverse replays.
source: (2) the symmetric STDP rule described by Mishra et al., 2016, in combination with cellular adaptation in CA3 PCs, provides an explanation for the coexistence of forward and reverse replays
evidence: Summary of findings from model manipulations, with citation to Mishra et al., 2016

claim: The pattern of strong connections in the network rather than the overall weight statistics may be critical for the emergence and key properties of SWRs and replay in area CA3.
source: (3) the pattern of strong connections in the network rather than the overall weight statistics may be critical for the emergence and key properties of SWRs and replay in area CA3
evidence: Summary of findings from model manipulations (binarized and shuffled weight matrices)

claim: Ripple oscillations are generated in the strongly driven, recurrently connected network of fast-spiking PVBCs by the FINO mechanism.
source: (4) ripple oscillations are generated in the strongly driven, recurrently connected network of fast-spiking PVBCs by the FINO mechanism (Schlingloff et al., 2014) (also known as PYR-INT-INT [Stark et al., 2014; Buzsáki, 2015; Ramirez-Villegas et al., 2018]).
evidence: Summary of findings from model manipulations, with citations to Schlingloff et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2014; Buzsáki, 2015; and Ramirez-Villegas et al., 2018

claim: SWRs represent the most synchronous physiological activity pattern with the largest excitatory gain in the mammalian brain.
source: SWRs represent the most synchronous physiological activity pattern with the largest excitatory gain in the mammalian brain (Buzsáki et al., 1983; Buzsáki et al., 1992; Buzsáki, 1989; Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzsáki et al., 1983; Buzsáki et al., 1992; Buzsáki, 1989; and Buzsáki, 2015

claim: Under normal conditions, ripples are typically observed riding on top of naturally emerging sharp waves.
source: Under normal conditions, ripples are typically observed riding on top of naturally emerging sharp waves.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge

claim: Schlingloff et al., 2014 and Stark et al., 2014 managed to decouple ripples from sharp waves by directly and indirectly activating the interconnected network of PVBCs using optogenetics.
source: More recently, using optogenetics, Schlingloff et al., 2014 and Stark et al., 2014 managed to decouple ripples from sharp waves by directly and indirectly activating the interconnected network of PVBCs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Schlingloff et al., 2014 and Stark et al., 2014

claim: Without drastic, nonphysiological modifications of the model, ripples were always tied to sequence replay, which was in turn associated with bouts of increased spiking activity in the network.
source: Our in silico results perfectly parallel this work: without drastic, nonphysiological modifications of the model ripples were always tied to sequence replay, which was in turn associated with bouts of increased spiking activity in the network (the sharp waves).
evidence: Observation from model simulations

claim: A relatively high (>2 Hz) mean firing rate in the PC population was required for inducing ripple oscillation in the model.
source: When we separated the PVBC network, we found that a relatively high (>2 Hz) mean firing rate in the PC population was required for inducing ripple oscillation, a condition that was satisfied only during sharp wave events and the associated sequence replay in our full baseline network.
evidence: Observation from the simplified PVBC network simulation

claim: The learned recurrent PC-PC synaptic weights are responsible for coding, govern sequence replay, and cause the ripples by giving rise to high PC activity during the replay.
source: Thus, the learned recurrent PC-PC synaptic weights are responsible for coding, govern sequence replay, and, by giving rise to high PC activity during the replay, they also cause the ripples.
evidence: Inference from model observations and manipulations

claim: Memory storage and recall, as well as the main hippocampal oscillations and transient activity patterns, are intimately interconnected in the model.
source: In summary, memory storage and recall, as well as the main hippocampal oscillations and transient activity patterns, are intimately interconnected in our unifying model.
evidence: Summary inference from model findings

claim: The model predicts that selectively blocking recurrent inhibitory connections between PVBCs should completely eliminate ripple oscillations, while having only minor quantitative effects on sharp waves and sequence replay.
source: As an important example, our model predicts that selectively blocking recurrent inhibitory connections between PVBCs should completely eliminate ripple oscillations, while having only minor quantitative effects (through modifying the effective gain of feedback inhibition of PCs) on sharp waves and sequence replay.
evidence: Prediction based on model manipulations

claim: Blocking or substantially attenuating recurrent excitatory interactions in area CA3 is expected to simultaneously eliminate sharp waves, ripple oscillations, and autonomous sequence replay.
source: By contrast, blocking or substantially attenuating recurrent excitatory interactions in area CA3 is expected to simultaneously eliminate sharp waves, ripple oscillations, and autonomous sequence replay.
evidence: Prediction based on model manipulations

claim: In the model, the nature of replayed sequences depends mostly on the activity patterns of hippocampal neurons during exploration, which determine, through learning, the subsequent pattern of recurrent interactions.
source: In our model, the nature of replayed sequences depends mostly on the activity patterns of hippocampal neurons during exploration, which determine, through learning, the subsequent pattern of recurrent interactions.
evidence: Inference from model design and observations

claim: A general prediction of the model framework is that one could deduce the nature of reactivations in different experiments using the same model simply by changing the spike statistics during the learning phase.
source: Overall, a general prediction of our framework is that one could deduce the nature of reactivations in different experiments using the same model simply by changing the spike statistics during the learning phase so that it mimics the corresponding experimental observations.
evidence: Prediction based on model framework

claim: The different results of replay studies should stem primarily from the different environments and protocols used during training rather than differences in analysis methods.
source: It also follows from this argument that the different results of these studies should stem primarily from the different environments and protocols used during training rather than, for instance, differences in analysis methods.
evidence: Inference from model framework

claim: In the model, the starting point and direction of replay depend on systematic biases and random variations in the weight structure, but also on spatio-temporal structure in the external inputs.
source: In our model, the starting point and direction of replay depend on systematic biases and random variations in the weight structure, but also on (random or deterministic) spatio-temporal structure in the external inputs.
evidence: Inference from model observations

claim: The model predicts that it should be possible to influence the starting point and direction of replay by the selective activation of place cells representing a particular location in offline states.
source: Although a detailed analysis of the relative impact of these factors will require further efforts, we can already make some predictions regarding the effects of various experimental manipulations. In particular, it should be possible to influence the starting point and direction of replay by the selective activation of place cells representing a particular location (or a sequence of locations) in offline states, although the rapid sequential activation of functionally defined chains of neurons might be technically challenging.
evidence: Prediction based on model observations

claim: The model predicts that manipulations of neuronal activity during exploration should have an impact on the content of replay and even on the global properties of sharp waves through their influence on the learned synaptic weight structure.
source: More importantly, our model also predicts that similar manipulations of neuronal activity during exploration should also have an impact on the content of replay, and even on the global properties of sharp waves, through their influence on the learned synaptic weight structure.
evidence: Prediction based on model framework

claim: The model predicts that it would be critical to explore whether the temporally symmetric STDP rule correctly describes the plasticity of CA3 excitatory recurrent collaterals under all physiological circumstances.
source: Finally, our modeling results also suggest that it would be critical to explore whether the unusual, temporally symmetric STDP rule uncovered by Mishra et al., 2016 correctly describes the plasticity of CA3 excitatory recurrent collaterals under all physiological circumstances, or perhaps the rule is different (not entirely symmetric or even antisymmetric) under some conditions in vivo, for example, depending on behavioral variables and the associated pattern of subcortical inputs.
evidence: Prediction based on model findings, with citation to Mishra et al., 2016

claim: The model predicts that any factors that change the symmetric nature of the plasticity rule during exploration should alter the balance of forward and backward replay events during subsequent SWRs.
source: One specific prediction of our model is that any factors that change the symmetric nature of the plasticity rule during exploration should alter the balance of forward and backward replay events during subsequent SWRs.
evidence: Prediction based on model findings

claim: The network model was constrained strongly by the available experimental data.
source: The network model presented here was constrained strongly by the available experimental data.
evidence: Statement about model construction methodology

claim: Many cellular and synaptic parameters were fit directly to in vitro measurements.
source: Many cellular and synaptic parameters were fit directly to in vitro measurements, and most functional parameters correspond to in vivo recordings of hippocampal place cells.
evidence: Statement about model construction methodology

claim: The 10% PC-PC connection probability is based on the classical viewpoint that considers the CA3 region as a highly interconnected network.
source: The 10% PC-PC connection probability is based on the classical viewpoint that considers the CA3 region as a highly interconnected network (Lisman, 1999; Andersen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lisman, 1999 and Andersen et al., 2007

claim: A recent physiological study estimated <1% connection probability in 400-µm-thick slices, but the authors concluded from virtual slicing experiments that recurrent axons were substantially reduced.
source: Although a recent physiological study (Guzman et al., 2016) estimated <1% connection probability in 400-µm-thick slices, the authors concluded from 'virtual slicing' experiments that recurrent axons were substantially reduced.
evidence: Supported by citation to Guzman et al., 2016

claim: Li et al., 1994 reported at least 70% axonal loss in 400 µm slices.
source: This is in agreement with Li et al., 1994, who reported at least 70% axonal loss in 400 µm slices.
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 1994

claim: The in vivo connection probability is likely to be considerably higher than 1%.
